analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Dodd-Frank Wall Street reform and consumer protection law in its entirety.
analysis.headline: A bill to repeal Dodd-Frank, backed by 29 Senate Republicans, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Dodd-Frank Act, the 2010 law passed after the 2008 financial crisis that tightened oversight of banks, regulated derivatives, and created a consumer financial watchdog. It would restore the laws as they existed before Dodd-Frank, returning banking rules to their pre-crisis state. It was introduced by Sen. Jim DeMint with 28 Republican cosponsors, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be large banks, securities and derivatives dealers, and consumer lenders, which would be freed from the capital requirements, derivatives clearing and trading rules, and consumer protections Dodd-Frank imposed. Banks had argued the law's compliance costs and restrictions made lending more expensive; removing them would raise bank profits and trading activity.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act in full and revives the laws as they existed before that Act was enacted.

Removal of Dodd-Frank's bank regulations would relieve banks of the capital, oversight, and consumer-protection requirements adopted after the 2008 financial crisis, an across-the-board reduction in regulatory cost for financial firms.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers, depositors, and taxpayers would bear the risk: the consumer watchdog, derivatives safeguards, and enhanced bank oversight created after the 2008 crisis would disappear, leaving households with fewer protections against the lending and trading practices that produced the crisis and the taxpayer-supported bailouts that followed it.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would eliminate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and all Dodd-Frank consumer protections, removing the federal agency charged with policing credit cards, mortgages, and other consumer financial products.

Repeal would strip away derivatives regulation and enhanced supervision of large banks, restoring the lighter pre-2008 rules under which risky lending and trading helped trigger the financial crisis and recession that cost millions of Americans jobs, homes, and savings.

The strongest objection supporters would raise is that Dodd-Frank's compliance burden fell hardest on smaller banks and that some of its rules tightened credit; repeal, however, would have removed the safeguards along with the paperwork, with no replacement framework.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered no partial fix: it repealed every Dodd-Frank provision and restored pre-crisis law wholesale. Whatever compliance costs Dodd-Frank imposed on banks, erasing consumer protections, derivatives safeguards, and crisis-resolution authorities in one stroke would have shifted the cost of financial risk back onto consumers and, in a crisis, taxpayers. The costs of this bill clearly outweighed its benefits for the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 31, 2011, and the committee never acted on it; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim DeMint introduced the bill on March 31, 2011, joined on the day of introduction by 18 original cosponsors including the Republican leader Sen. Mitch McConnell.
A total of 28 Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the post-2008 financial safeguards stayed on the books. Bank customers and taxpayers kept the consumer watchdog and bank oversight Dodd-Frank created; the banks and lenders that would have gained from repeal got nothing.

for.name: Jim DeMint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal Dodd-Frank in its entirety and led its cosponsorship effort.

for.name: 28 of 51 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the full repeal, including Republican leader Mitch McConnell.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support; the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Full repeal would have removed the capital requirements, enhanced supervision, and resolution authorities Dodd-Frank imposed after the 2008 crisis, restoring lighter pre-crisis rules and higher potential profitability. Ordinary consumers would bear the added risk of the practices those rules restrain.

Repeal would have eliminated Dodd-Frank's derivatives regulation — clearing, exchange trading, and recordkeeping requirements — freeing dealers to trade as they did before 2010. Those rules exist to keep complex bets from cascading into a taxpayer-backed crisis.

Repeal would have abolished the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, removing federal policing of credit cards, mortgages, payday lending, and debt collection. Lenders would face fewer constraints on practices that charge or squeeze consumers.
